title: 507 Mechanical Movements
why: A Victorian catalogue of clever mechanisms, now animated. Most of them could be printed.

title: Mathematical sculpture
why: Henry Segerman prints shapes that explain hard maths, such as shadows that turn into grids.

title: Compliant mechanisms
why: Parts that bend instead of using hinges, so a whole machine can be one printed piece.

title: Photogrammetry
why: Walk around an object taking photos and free software turns them into a 3D model.

title: Strandbeests
why: Theo Jansen's wind-powered walking sculptures. Small printed versions walk across a desk.

title: Auxetic materials
why: Structures that get fatter when you stretch them. Easy to print, strange to hold.

title: The gyroid
why: That wavy infill pattern is a real mathematical surface, and it also appears in butterfly wings.

title: The Miura fold
why: A way of folding a sheet so it opens in one pull. Used for maps and for solar panels in space.

title: Lithophanes
why: Thin panels that look like nothing until lit from behind, when a photograph appears.

title: Voronoi diagrams
why: The pattern in giraffe skin, dragonfly wings and cracked mud, and in a lot of printed lamps.

title: Tensegrity
why: Structures where the solid parts never touch and seem to float, held only by tension.

title: Automata
why: Hand-cranked mechanical figures, some centuries old, that write, draw or play music.

title: Lost-wax casting
why: A 6,000-year-old way to turn a model into metal. A printed part can stand in for the wax.

title: Printed buildings
why: The same idea as a desktop printer, scaled up to squeeze out houses in concrete.

title: RepRap
why: The project that set out to build a printer able to print its own parts, and started the hobby.

title: Museum objects in 3D
why: The Smithsonian has scanned fossils, spacecraft and statues that you can turn around on screen.

title: Burr puzzles
why: Interlocking notched sticks that slide apart only in one order. A good test of print tolerances.

title: Topology optimisation
why: Software removes every bit of material a part does not need. The results look like bone.

title: The Antikythera mechanism
why: A geared astronomical calculator from ancient Greece. People now build working replicas.

title: Bioprinting
why: Printers that lay down living cells in place of plastic, in the hope of building tissue.
